text: Do veterans and retirees get SCRA or MLA benefits?

spans.text: Both laws protect active-duty servicemembers only. SCRA requests can be filed up to roughly 180 days after separation for pre-service debt, and then the window closes; MLA coverage ends with active service. One practical nuance: fees on cards you opened while on active duty may not resume the moment you separate — issuers periodically re-check the DoD database — but plan your budget as if every fee returns. text: FREQUENTLY ASKED QUESTIONS

question: What credit cards waive the annual fee for military?

spans.text: American Express, Chase, Citi, and U.S. Bank waive annual fees on personal cards for active-duty servicemembers under both SCRA and MLA — MLA also covers military spouses on their own cards. Capital One waives fees only under SCRA, which means the account must have been opened before active duty began. Navy Federal waives its $49 Flagship fee only under SCRA. Veterans and retirees are not covered by either law.

question: Does American Express waive annual fees for military?

spans.text: Yes. American Express waives annual fees on all personal cards for active-duty servicemembers under both SCRA and MLA. MLA relief is applied automatically when an eligible servicemember or spouse opens a card during active duty; SCRA relief on pre-service accounts must be requested. Military spouses qualify for the MLA waiver on their own cards, not just as authorized users.

question: Does Chase waive credit card fees for military spouses?

spans.text: Yes. Under the Military Lending Act, spouses of active-duty servicemembers are "covered borrowers," so a spouse can open their own Chase personal card — including the Sapphire Reserve or Preferred — and have the annual fee waived. There is no requirement to be an authorized user; separate accounts also mean each spouse can earn their own welcome offer. Chase verifies MLA status automatically against the Department of Defense database.

question: What is the difference between SCRA and MLA?

spans.text: SCRA (the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act) applies to credit you opened BEFORE active duty: it caps interest at 6% on pre-service debt, counts fees as interest, and must be requested. MLA (the Military Lending Act) applies to credit you open DURING active duty: it caps the Military APR at 36%, is applied automatically, and covers spouses and dependents enrolled in DEERS. Because annual fees count toward the 36% MAPR, major issuers simply waive them on MLA-covered accounts.

question: Do veterans get SCRA or MLA credit card benefits?

spans.text: No. Both laws protect servicemembers on active duty only. SCRA relief can be requested up to 180 days after leaving active duty for debt incurred before service, but once that window closes the protections end, and MLA coverage ends when active service ends. Veterans should optimize for rewards and no-annual-fee cards instead — or credit-union programs like PenFed’s Honors Advantage, which explicitly includes honorably discharged veterans.

question: Does Capital One waive the Venture X annual fee for active duty?

spans.text: Only under SCRA — never under MLA. That means the Venture X (or any Capital One card) must have been opened before your active-duty period began; open it during active duty and you will pay the $395 fee. Capital One’s SCRA program caps interest at 4%, better than the statutory 6%, and one request covers Discover accounts too, since Discover is now part of Capital One.

question: Do military credit card fee waivers apply to National Guard and Reserve?

spans.text: Yes, while on qualifying orders. Guard and Reserve members serving on active orders of 30 or more consecutive days (Title 10, or Title 32 for SCRA-covered National Guard service) are treated as active duty for these protections, as are commissioned officers of the Public Health Service and NOAA. One practical play for Capital One cards: open the card before a qualifying activation, then request SCRA once on orders.

question: What is the maximum interest rate on a credit card for active-duty military?

spans.text: Two caps apply. Under SCRA, interest on debt you incurred before active duty is capped at 6% — and fees count as interest, with the excess forgiven, not deferred. Under MLA, credit opened during active duty is capped at a 36% Military APR (MAPR), which also counts most fees. Several issuers voluntarily beat the SCRA cap: Capital One, Navy Federal, and USAA all cap covered accounts at 4%.

question: Is the Amex Platinum worth it for military?

spans.text: For active-duty servicemembers, it is one of the strongest cards available: the $895 annual fee is waived under both SCRA and MLA, so you keep the lounge access and the card’s long menu of statement credits at no annual cost. A spouse can hold their own fee-waived Platinum under MLA. For veterans, the math changes — no waiver applies, so it is only worth it if you actually use enough of the credits and travel benefits to beat the fee.

question: What happens to my credit cards when I leave active duty?

spans.text: MLA and SCRA fee waivers end when your covered status ends, so plan for annual fees to return. In practice fees may not resume immediately — issuers periodically re-check the DoD database — but budget as if they will. Before separation, decide card by card: keep the ones whose benefits beat the fee, downgrade the rest to no-fee versions rather than canceling, and avoid closing your oldest account, which shortens your credit history.
